sentences: After performing an open heart surgery, the surgeon, a cardiothoracic surgeon in a midwestern city, goes to a diner where he meets 16-year-old the teenager, whose father died a few years earlier.
The surgeon invites the teenager to meet his family—comprising his wife the mother, their daughter the girl, and their son the young boy.
The teenager makes a good impression on everyone, but seems to especially get along with the girl.
The following night, the surgeon goes to the teenager's house for dinner at the teenager's request.

After the teenager goes to bed, the teenager's mother initiates sex with the surgeon; when he rejects her, she tells him that it is the teenager's wish for them to have sex, after which the surgeon angrily leaves.
The teenager visits the surgeon's office, complaining of chest pain.
The surgeon runs tests on the teenager, all of which produce normal results.
The teenager invites the surgeon over again, but the surgeon declines.

The teenager's demands for the surgeon's attention grow increasingly frequent and desperate, and the surgeon becomes gradually more frustrated and concerned, especially when he learns that the teenager gave the girl a ride home on his motorcycle.
One morning, the young boy finds himself unable to move his legs.
The surgeon and the mother rush him to the hospital, where numerous tests are performed.
The teenager then reveals that his father died while the surgeon was operating on him.

The teenager blames the surgeon for his death and believes that to make things even, the surgeon must kill a member of his own family; if the surgeon refuses, all four will eventually die within a few days, beginning with paralysis, an inability to eat, and finally bleeding from the eyes.
The surgeon has the teenager ejected from the hospital.
Later, the young boy begins inexplicably refusing to eat, even when the surgeon begins furiously forcing him to.
The girl, who has fallen in love with the teenager, collapses while singing in her school's choir and is also hospitalized.
When she also starts rejecting food, she and the young boy are both given feeding tubes.
The surgeon finally confides in the mother about his history with the teenager, eventually admitting that he had consumed alcohol before performing the teenager's father's surgery.
The teenager phones the girl, instructing her to stand up and walk.
She complies, only to become paralyzed again when he hangs up.
The mother, witnessing this, confronts the teenager and proclaims that he has no right to force her children to suffer.
The teenager asserts that this is merely justice for his father.
The girl and the young boy are discharged.
After the mother chastises the surgeon for his passive attitude toward their situation, the surgeon ties the teenager up in their basement, beats him, and shoots his legs.
Unintimidated, the teenager bites the surgeon's arm, before biting his own arm as an example of retributive justice.
The girl and the young boy argue over which one of them the surgeon will kill, and each try to respectively curry his favor.
The surgeon asks their school principal which of the two is better, though the principal cannot provide an answer.
Back home, the mother takes the children to see the teenager, where she tends to his wounds and kisses his feet, ultimately failing to elicit any sympathy from him.
She encourages the surgeon to kill one of the children rather than her, as they can have another child.
The girl implores the teenager to heal her so they can run away together; when this fails, she tells the surgeon how much she loves her family and offers her life to spare theirs.
Hopeless, the mother finally releases the teenager.
When the young boy begins bleeding from his eyes, the surgeon places him, the girl, and the mother in a circle, bound with duct tape, and covers their heads.
The surgeon pulls a wool hat over his own face and repeatedly fires a rifle while spinning in a circle.
He narrowly misses the girl and the mother, but the third shot kills the young boy.
Some time later, the teenager enters the diner where he and the surgeon used to meet, where the remaining family members are.
The three promptly leave, with the mother and the girl glaring at the teenager, while the surgeon avoids his gaze.
In the late spring of 1959, the peaceful, all-white neighborhood of the suburb is shaken by the arrival of the black newcomer family.
The father, a seemingly mild-mannered family man, lives in the suburb with his paraplegic wife, the mother, and their son, the boy.

One night when the mother's identical twin sister, the aunt, is staying over, two robbers, the first intruder and the second intruder, break into his house, tie the whole family up, and knock them out with chloroform.
The mother receives an overdose and never regains consciousness.
After the funeral, the aunt moves in to help take care of the boy and soon begins to transform herself into the mother, dyeing her hair blonde and having sex with the father.

The family are called to the police station to identify the first intruder and the second intruder, but both the father and the aunt say the police have the wrong men, even though the boy recognizes them as his mother's murderers.
Soon after this, the first intruder and the second intruder show up at the father's job and demand the money he owes them as payment for killing the mother.
When the father refuses to pay, they make plans to kill the boy and the aunt.

With tensions mounting between the residents of the suburb and their new black neighbors the newcomer family, charismatic insurance agent the investigator arrives on the family's doorstep one day when the father is not home and begins to question the aunt.

He initially says he is simply looking to clear up red flags in a life insurance claim the father made on the mother, but eventually admits to the aunt that he suspects her and the father of murdering the mother to collect on the policy, at which point the aunt kicks him out of the house.
That night, as the protracted protest at the newcomer family's home turns into a riot, the investigator returns to talk with the father.
He tells the father that he knows the nature of his and the aunt's insurance-fraud plan and attempts to blackmail them into giving him their entire payout in exchange for his silence.
The aunt poisons his coffee with lye, and the father bashes his head in with a fireplace poker to finish him off.
The father leaves to hide the body, trailed by the first intruder.
The aunt attempts to kill the boy with a poisoned sandwich and milk after she catches him calling his uncle for help, but he refuses to leave his room.
The second intruder enters and strangles the aunt to death.
He heads upstairs to murder the boy, but the uncle arrives just in time and shoots the second intruder dead.
The uncle gives the boy his gun and hides the boy in a closet before succumbing to a stab wound inflicted by the second intruder.

On the way home from disposing of the investigator's body, the father is taunted by the first intruder, who is suddenly hit and killed by a fire truck that was speeding to a fire started by the rioters at the newcomer family's home.
At his own house, he discovers the bodies of the aunt, the uncle, and the second intruder, and finds the boy in the closet.

The father offers the boy a choice: to go along with his plan to take the insurance money and run away to a tropical island, or die, with the father claiming his son was yet another of the second intruder's victims.
The next morning, the father is dead, having consumed the poisoned sandwich and milk during his conversation with the boy.

The boy calmly goes outside to play ball with the neighbor boy, the young son of the newcomer family whom he has befriended, while his parents and a few members of the community clean up the mess left in the wake of the riot.
The lead detective and the junior detective pursue the criminal, who claims that he must start a "game" in exchange for his own survival.
He activates a remote trigger, and is then shot and collapses.
Five people – the first man, the first woman, the second man, the second woman, and an unconscious man – awaken inside a barn with buckets on their heads and chains around their necks.
A tape recording from the mastermind explains that they must each sacrifice blood to survive before the chains pull them towards a wall of buzzsaws.
Most of the group escapes by cutting themselves, except for the unconscious man, who awakens too late.
Their next test reveals that the second woman, a purse snatcher, accidentally caused the death of an asthmatic woman.
To save the others from being hanged, she must inject herself with one of three needles – one an antidote to a poison in her system, another being saline, and the last one acid.
She refuses, so the second man injects her with all three, killing her but saving the others.
In their third test, the second man attempts to escape the barn, but his leg falls through loose floorboards, and is ensnared by wires.
Another tape recorder reveals that he will be punished for breaking the rules and must pull a lever to be "set free."
The first woman and the first man become trapped inside a silo, forcing the second man to pull the lever and sever his leg to rescue them.
The lead detective and the junior detective investigate the discovery of corpses that appear to be the unconscious man and the second woman, whose deaths fit the mastermind's modus operandi.
The lead detective becomes suspicious of pathologists the male pathologist and the female pathologist.
The female pathologist reveals to the male pathologist that she is a trap killer fangirl, but now fears this might incriminate her.
The junior detective spies and informs the lead detective.
Later, the criminal is abducted from the hospital.

In the barn, the first man is revealed to have sold a faulty motorcycle to the mastermind's nephew, causing his death, and is tested by being lowered into a funnel with a spiral-shaped blade powered by a motorcycle engine inside.
He attempts to stop the blade, but is ultimately killed.
The criminal's corpse is found inside the mastermind's grave.
The lead detective finds a corpse appearing to be the first man in the female pathologist's studio and calls for her and the male pathologist's arrest.

The male pathologist convinces the junior detective to let them go after saying that the bullet which hit the criminal was fired by the lead detective, whom he and the female pathologist suspect to be the new trap killer.
The female pathologist deduces the game's location and she and the male pathologist depart for the barn, with the lead detective in pursuit.
In the barn, the first woman and the second man are shackled to pipes at opposite ends of a room.

The mastermind confronts them and reveals that the first woman asphyxiated her baby and framed her husband, who later committed suicide, and the second man's drunken tomfoolery caused his friends' death in a car accident.
Meanwhile, the junior detective finds jigsaw-shaped pieces of flesh in the lead detective's freezer.
For their final test, the mastermind leaves the two a shotgun loaded with one shell, saying it is their key to freedom.
The lead detective ambushes the male pathologist and the female pathologist at the barn.
The first woman tries to shoot the second man, but the gun backfires, killing her.
The second man finds the now-destroyed keys among the debris; they had been hidden inside the shell.
The female pathologist escapes the lead detective, while an unseen assailant drugs him.
The male pathologist and the lead detective awaken in collars rigged with laser cutters and are told to confess their sins.
The lead detective forces the male pathologist to go first; the male pathologist confesses to mislabeling the mastermind's X-rays years earlier, causing his cancer to go undiagnosed.
Despite confessing, the male pathologist is apparently killed.
The lead detective then admits to allowing criminals to walk free for personal gain and his collar deactivates.
The male pathologist is revealed to still be alive, and also the unconscious man from the first barn game, which took place ten years earlier.
Feeling that the male pathologist should not die because of an honest mistake, the mastermind saved him and recruited him as his first apprentice.

The male pathologist reveals that he recreated the barn games, chose his victims from other criminals that the lead detective let go, and framed the lead detective as the new trap killer as revenge for releasing the criminal, who killed the male pathologist's wife.
For breaking the rules by forcing the male pathologist to go first, the lead detective's collar is reactivated, slicing his head open.
The male pathologist says, "I speak for the dead," before shutting the door and leaving.
In 1934, famed Belgian detective the sleuth solves a theft at a famous church in a holy city.
Intending to return to a distant capital, his friend the railway official arranges accommodations for the sleuth aboard the alpine-route train, the luxury express.

Alongside the railway official, the sleuth's fellow passengers include widow the matron; businessman the tycoon, his manservant the valet and secretary the assistant; the elderly Russian princess and her maid the servant; Hungarian diplomat the count and his wife the countess; physician the doctor; the teacher, a governess; the devout woman, a Spanish missionary; Cuban-American car salesman the car dealer; and the academic, an Austrian university professor.
Having received threatening letters, the tycoon attempts to hire the sleuth to protect him during the journey, but the sleuth declines, not wanting to do business with a suspicious character.
An avalanche derails the train's engine, stranding the passengers until a rescue crew can re-rail the locomotive.
During the night, the sleuth is awakened by strange noises in the hall next to his cabin and sees someone in a red kimono rushing down the aisleway.
The tycoon is found murdered the following morning, stabbed a dozen times.
The sleuth and the railway official work together to hunt the murderer.

The sleuth discovers the burned remnants of one of the tycoon's threatening notes, and from it deduces that the tycoon was really the kidnapper, the man responsible for the kidnap and murder of the little girl, an infant child.
The little girl's death caused her mother, the bereaved mother, to go into premature labour, killing her and the baby, and out of grief her father, the colonel, killed himself.
The family maid, the housemaid, accused of complicity in the little girl's murder, also committed suicide.
The sleuth finds a bloodstained handkerchief with a monogrammed "H", and a conductor uniform button in the matron's cabin, leading him to find the uniform and kimono planted in his suitcase.
The matron is later stabbed from behind and cannot identify the culprit.
The sleuth's interrogations of the passengers identifies direct connections between them and the bereaved family.
While interviewing the teacher, the sleuth is shot in the shoulder by the doctor, who confesses to the murder; the railway official incapacitates him before he can kill the sleuth.
However, the sleuth quickly surmises that the doctor, a former skilled army sniper, deliberately missed a killing shot.

The sleuth gathers and confronts the passengers outside the train, uncovering their true identities: the assistant's district attorney father was pressured into prosecuting the housemaid, but his career was destroyed when she was posthumously exonerated.
The academic, in actuality a former police officer named the ex-policeman, was in love with the housemaid.
The crewman, the train's conductor, was the housemaid's brother.
The doctor and the terminally ill valet were the colonel's comrades.
The car dealer, the servant, and the devout woman worked for the bereaved family as their chauffeur, cook, and nursemaid respectively.
The countess is the bereaved mother's sister, the aunt.
The teacher was the little girl's and the aunt's governess.
The princess was the little girl's godmother.
The matron is actually the performer, a former stage actress, the bereaved mother's and the aunt's mother, and the little girl's grandmother.
The sleuth concludes that they murdered the kidnapper together, each stabbing him once.
The matron takes the blame for planning the murder and recruiting the others.
The teacher wore the kimono and the doctor superficially stabbed the matron to mislead the sleuth.
Agreeing their cause was just, but compelled to tell the truth, the sleuth challenges the passengers to shoot him dead so they will get away with the murder.
Instead, the matron grabs the gun and attempts suicide, but realises it is unloaded; the sleuth was testing the suspects' characters.
With the locomotive back on the tracks, the sleuth surmises that justice is impossible in this case, as the kidnapper deserved death.
For the first time, the sleuth must live with a lie and imbalance.
He presents the lone escaped killer theory to the Yugoslavian police, allowing the others to remain on the train.
As he disembarks, a British army messenger delivers a note asking him to investigate a death on a famous river.
In the Mexican town of the home town, a young woman named the matriarch marries a man who eventually leaves her and their daughter the great-grandmother to pursue a music career.
When he never returns, the matriarch bans music from her family and opens a shoemaking business.
Decades later, the matriarch's great-great-grandson the boy lives in the family home with his parents and relatives, including an elderly and ailing great-grandmother.
Despite the family's continued ban on music, the boy secretly loves it and teaches himself to play guitar by watching the VHS documentary of his idol, the late musician the star.
On the Day of the Dead, the boy inadvertently bumps the family ofrenda and breaks a frame containing a photo of the matriarch and an infant great-grandmother.
He discovers a hidden section of the photograph that shows his great-great-grandfather, whose head has been torn from the photo, holding the star's famous guitar.
Believing this proves the star is his relative, the boy excitedly tells his family about his musical aspirations.
In response, the boy's grandmother, the household head, destroys his guitar, causing him to shun his family.
The boy breaks into the star's mausoleum and takes his guitar to use in a local talent competition.
Once the boy strums it, he becomes invisible to all living people.
However, he can interact with his skeletal dead relatives, who are visiting from the afterlife for the holiday.
Taking him back with them, they realize the matriarch cannot visit since the boy removed her photo from the ofrenda.
The boy also discovers that he has been cursed for stealing from the dead: he must receive a family blessing to return to the living world before sunrise or he will remain in the afterlife forever.
The matriarch offers him a blessing on the condition that he abandons music, but the boy refuses and seeks the star's blessing instead.
The boy encounters the drifter, a down-on-his-luck trickster skeleton who once performed with the star.

The drifter offers to bring the boy to the star in exchange for the boy placing his photo on an ofrenda so he can visit his daughter before she forgets him, which would cause him to fade from existence.
The drifter helps the boy perform in a talent competition to win entry to the star's mansion, but the boy flees after being discovered by his family.
The boy sneaks into the star's mansion and is welcomed by a surprised star, but the drifter appears and accuses the star of stealing his songs.
As the two argue, the boy slowly pieces together the truth: the star and the drifter were once a musical act on the brink of fame until the drifter grew homesick and tried to leave.
Unable to write songs himself, the star poisoned the drifter and stole his guitar and songs to pass off as his own.
To protect his legacy, the star seizes the drifter's photo and has the boy and the drifter thrown into a cenote pit.
There, the drifter reveals that his daughter is named the great-grandmother, thus making him the boy's actual great-great-grandfather.
After being rescued by his family, the boy reveals the truth about the drifter's death, and the matriarch, though she is angry at the drifter, agrees to help him.
The family infiltrates the star's concert to retrieve the drifter's photo.
The star's crimes are exposed to the audience, who quickly turn on him, and he is crushed by a falling bell, mirroring his fate in real life, although the drifter's photograph is lost in the chaos.
As the sun rises, the matriarch and a fading drifter unconditionally bless the boy and return him to the living world.
Back home, the boy plays "the famous song" on the drifter's guitar, brightening the great-grandmother to sing with him.
She shares that she kept the torn piece of the photo with the drifter's face, then tells her family stories about her father, preserving his memory and existence in the afterlife.
The boy reconciles with his family and their ban on music is finally lifted.

One year later, the boy shows his new baby sister the family ofrenda, now displaying photos of the drifter and a recently deceased great-grandmother, while the great-grandmother's collected letters from the drifter prove the star's theft of his songs, leading to the star's disgrace and the drifter's rightful recognition.
In the afterlife, the drifter joins the matriarch, the great-grandmother, and their family to visit the living world.
The boy performs a heartfelt song for both his living and dead relatives.
In mid-1950s the capital, the young woman, granddaughter of the late Greek-born business tycoon the old man, visits private investigator the detective.
She asks the detective to investigate the old man's death, suspecting that he has been murdered.
The detective agrees reluctantly, feeling conflicted due to an earlier love affair with the young woman in the foreign city.
The detective seeks the consent of the chief inspector of the police headquarters to look into the case.
The old man had been the bullying and manipulative patriarch of the large and idiosyncratic tycoon's family who all lived together on the family estate.
He had died from a heart attack after his regular insulin injection – given by his wife the widow – had been laced with eserine from his eye drops.
The widow is the old man's second wife, a former casino dancer who is much younger than her husband.
The great-aunt is the sister of the old man's late first wife, fond of stalking the grounds and blasting moles in the lawn with a shotgun.
She despised her brother-in-law.

The old man's elder son, the writer, hated his father for passing him over as successor to the family business, and for refusing to fund production of a screenplay he wrote for his wife, the actress, a fading theatre actress.

Their children (the old man's grandchildren) are the young woman, the grandson, a cynical rock'n'roll-loving teenager affected by polio, and the little girl, a clever 12-year-old who knows everyone's business.
The younger son, the businessman, is managing director of a major family business, but is a failure who has required multiple bailouts.
His domineering wife the scientist is a plant biologist with extensive knowledge of poisons.
The tutor, a private tutor, has been having an affair with the widow.
He is spied upon by his pupil the little girl from her tree house hideout.
The detective interviews the family and is met with hostility.
All of the family members have motives for the killing: all resented the old man's bullying and manipulative ways, and are now expecting a sizeable bequest.
Most suspect the widow, as the outsider who had administered the fatal injection.
Their suspicions are strengthened when it transpires that the old man's will was unsigned, resulting in the widow inheriting his entire estate under the intestacy rules.
The little girl hints that she has found clues, but will not disclose them.
The ladder to the little girl's tree house is sabotaged, and she falls and is knocked unconscious.
Suspicion switches to the young woman after another, properly signed, will is discovered, leaving the whole estate to her.
The chief inspector arrives to take over the case; he feels the detective's history with the young woman compromises him.
The discovery of love letters between the widow and the tutor gives the chief inspector enough evidence to arrest them for the old man's murder and the attempt on the little girl's life.
The detective, however, remains unconvinced.
The little girl is angry that her private notebook has disappeared.
Her nanny prepares hot chocolate for her.
The little girl refuses the drink, and her nanny dies after drinking it herself.
The detective implores the little girl to name the killer.
Again, the little girl refuses, even when the detective warns her that she is in danger.
The great-aunt is diagnosed with a fatal illness, and is told she has only months to live.
The coroner finds that the nanny had died of cyanide poisoning.
The detective suspects the great-aunt, who used cyanide to kill moles.
He searches the great-aunt's garden shed and finds a bottle of cyanide, as well as the little girl's missing notebook, buried in quicklime.
The great-aunt takes the little girl into the countryside for a drive.
She leaves a note confessing to the murders.
The detective and the young woman chase them in another car.
As they drive, the young woman reads from the little girl's notebook and discovers the truth: that the little girl had murdered the old man for having stopped her ballet lessons.
She had also staged her fall from the tree house, poisoned the nanny (who had begun to suspect her), and forged the widow's love letters.
The great-aunt had realised that the little girl was the killer and falsely confessed to exonerate the widow and the tutor, and to spare the little girl a life in psychiatric institutions.
The accused woman, a young actress in a travelling theatre troupe, is found in a daze with blood on her clothes, sitting by the murdered body of another young actress, the victim.
The poker used to commit the murder is at the accused woman's feet, but she has no memory of what happened during the minutes that the crime was committed.
The two young women are thought to have been rivals, and the police arrest her.
The accused woman withholds some important information deliberately, to protect something about the identity of a man that she will not name.
At her trial, most of the jury are certain she is guilty.

One or two feel that she may have a severe mental illness which means that she really does have no memory of killing the other woman, but they are convinced that she should still be hanged lest she strike again.
One juror, the famous actor, a celebrated actor-manager, seems sure she must be innocent, but is brow-beaten into voting "guilty" along with the rest of the jury.
The accused woman is imprisoned, and awaits hanging.
The famous actor feels responsible, as he had recommended that the accused woman take the touring job in order for her to get more experience.
He discovers the accused woman has been a fan of his since childhood, and considers her far too honest and straightforward to be a criminal of any kind.
Using skills he has learned in the theatre, the famous actor investigates the murder with the help of the stage manager the assistant and his wife the assistant's wife.
They narrow the possible suspects down to a male actor in the troupe, the suspect.

During a prison visit with the accused woman, the famous actor learns the suspect's secret: he is half-caste and passing as white, and the victim had threatened to expose him to the accused woman, with whom he was in love, neither of them knowing that the accused woman already knew this.
The famous actor cunningly tries to lure a confession out of the suspect, by asking him to audition for a new play he has been writing.
The famous actor describes a plot closely resembling the murder, and the suspect realises that they know he committed the crime and understand how and why he did it.
The suspect leaves without confessing and returns to his previous job as a transvestite trapeze performer in a circus.
The famous actor and the others go there to confront him again.
During the suspect's performance, he looks down and sees them waiting.
Despairing, he knots his access rope into a noose, slips it over his head, and jumps to his death.
The famous actor and the assistant discover the suspect had written a confession to the murder before his suicide.
At the film's conclusion, the accused woman is shown free and glamorously dressed in a white fur, entering a beautiful room and being welcomed warmly by the famous actor, who receives her lovingly.
The camera pulls back and reveals this is the last scene of a new play, possibly the new play, in which the accused woman stars opposite the famous actor.
They kiss as the curtain falls.
The young man returns from a seaside holiday and discovers a camera has mysteriously appeared in his car.
When he develops the negatives, one of the photos appears to show a man stabbing another.
The others offer clues to where the event took place.
A man tries to steal the camera from the young man, and takes the negative.
After identifying the location of a woman in one of the photos, the young man tracks down the young woman, whose missing brother, the photographer, took the photos before disappearing.
She and he go on a search through the countryside to try to locate her missing brother.
As they investigate, they discover the photographer may be involved in a jewel robbery and murder, and the police also appear to be on his trail.
This leads them to a local inn, where the young woman misleads the young man, and later confesses that she was protecting her brother.
They find evidence that the photographer was trying to expose the thieves involved in the robbery, by setting up his camera to capture evidence of them.
The camera photographed the fatal struggle of the thieves and the photographer fled, dropping the camera in the young man's car.
The photographer is arrested but later confesses his role in the crime.
The young man, suspecting that the policeman investigating the case might actually be the murderer, confronts him and uncovers the truth.
The murderer is caught, the photographer is released, and the young man and the young woman, now in love, become engaged.
The captain and the other captain are best friends.
The other captain is in love with the woman, and he brings the captain to the port city to meet her.
However, the captain and the woman fall in love with one another.
Both men propose to her on the same day.
The woman chooses the captain.
The woman and the captain reveal their marriage plans to the other captain and he gets furious with jealousy, and believes the captain has deceived him.
The captain tells him that he will marry the woman even if it means the end of their friendship.
As the couple plans to sail, the captain is short of crew.
He asks the other captain to forgive him and help.
The other captain agrees and sends a man, the henchman, not to help, but to do something to the ship.
The captain also recruits other men, including the troubled sailor, who is a sailor who has suffered a lot and is about to have a mental breakdown.
As the voyage begins, the crew realizes that there is a murderer among them who is killing them off one by one.
Meanwhile, a crew member tries to rape the woman; the troubled sailor saves her by killing the man.
But then he cries because he cannot stand the pain of killing a man.
Soon, everybody has died or disappeared except the first mate, the troubled sailor and a third crew member, the deckhand.
They decide that one of them must be the killer.
The deckhand realizes that the troubled sailor could not kill because he is too soft, so he runs after the first mate.
The first mate shoots the deckhand and then celebrates with the troubled sailor on becoming the new captain of the ship, and makes plans for the future.

The troubled sailor gets angry and tells the first mate that he was shanghaied six years before, on the same ship, and, due to his horrific treatment aboard at that time, committed the murders to get revenge.
He shoots the first mate and throws him into the sea.
Just after killing the first mate, the troubled sailor is hit on the head by the ship's boom.
When he regains consciousness, he runs everywhere on the ship searching for the first mate, then, in his madness, jumps overboard.
The ship drifts with the wind until it is spotted by another ship.
The ship is totally abandoned except for a black cat.
A final scene shows the other captain handing money to a crew member, commenting "I am thinking of the captain and her, dead!"
On a stormy night, at a retreat on the English coast, the film star, a successful actress, argues passionately with her jealous ex-husband the musician.
Not accepting her overseas divorce as valid, he accuses her of having an affair.
Finally, she slaps him and he leaves the room.
His eyes twitch violently.
The next morning, writer the young man is walking along the seaside when the film star's dead body washes ashore.
He recognizes her, and runs for help.
Two young women arrive just in time to see him racing away from the corpse.
The police quickly decide that the young man is the only suspect.
The film star was strangled with the belt from a raincoat; his raincoat is missing and he says it was recently stolen.
He admits having known the film star for three years since he sold her a story.
The police headquarters detectives grill him all night.
They suggest he was having an affair with the film star.
When they tell him she left him a large sum of money in her will, he faints.
He is revived with the aid of the young woman, daughter of the local police Chief Constable.
The young man is assigned an incompetent solicitor, and is taken into court for his formal arraignment.
Doubting if his innocence will ever be established, he takes advantage of overcrowding in the courthouse to escape.
He gets away by riding on the running board of the young woman's small car, revealing himself to her after the car runs out of petrol.
He helps push the car to a filling station, pays for petrol, and convinces her to give him a ride.
Though she is initially fearful and unsure about her passenger, the young woman eventually becomes convinced of his innocence and decides to help him.
They are eventually spotted together, forcing both to stay on the run from the police.
The young man tries to prove his innocence by tracking down the stolen coat: if it still has its belt, the one found next to the film star's body must not be his.
The duo succeed in tracing the young man's coat to the tramp, a homeless china-mender.
But the tramp was not the thief; he was given the coat by a man with "twitchy eyes", and with its belt already missing.
After becoming separated from the others, the young woman is taken in by the police.
Upon realizing that his daughter has fully allied herself with a murder suspect, her father chooses to resign his position rather than arrest her for assisting a felon.
The young man sneaks into their house to see the young woman, intending to surrender and assert he kidnapped her, but she mentions that the coat had a box of matches from the big hotel in a pocket.
As the young man has never been there, he surmises perhaps the murderer has a connection to the hotel.
The following evening, the young woman and the tramp go to the hotel together, hoping to find him.
It is revealed that the musician is the drummer in the band in the hotel ballroom, performing in blackface.
His eyes are twitching.
Recognizing the tramp in the audience, and seeing policemen nearby (who have actually followed the tramp, hoping he would lead them to the young man), the musician performs poorly due to fear.
He is berated by the conductor and, during a break, takes medicine to try to control the twitching, but it makes him very sleepy.
Eventually, in mid-performance, the musician passes out, drawing the attention of the young woman and the police.
Immediately after being revived and confronted, he confesses his crime and begins laughing hysterically.
With the young man exonerated, the young woman happily introduces him to her father.
